Pursue your radiant sun, sorrowful shadow,
Even though you are dark as the nighttime
While she is fashioned entirely from brightness,
Still, chase after your radiant sun, sorrowful shadow.

Chase after the one whose brilliance strips away your own,
Though you dwell here in shame and dishonor,
While she has been set up in the heavens,
Still, pursue the one whose glow brings the world back to life.

Trail behind those unspoiled rays whose loveliness sets things aflame,
The very ones that have singed and scorched you,
So that you must remain forever dark,
Until Her gentle rays convert your darkness into shining light.

Follow her now, while her splendor still glows,
For an unfortunate night is approaching
That will darken and diminish all her radiance,
And this the gloomy, sorrowful shadow foresees.

Keep following, since your destiny has commanded it this way,
For the Sun is bound to possess his shadow,
Until the two of them vanish together in the same instant—
The Sun always vindicated, the shadow always scorned.

Poetry Out Loud Note: In the printed collection, this poem carries the title "Follow thy fair sun, unhappy shadow." The reciter is permitted to announce either title while performing.
outputs.L3:
**The Shadow and the Sun**

Follow, unhappy shadow, follow still your fair sun, and do not turn away, though you are dark as night itself while she is fashioned wholly out of light. Let no despair make you abandon her, for in her presence lies your only purpose, and in her radiance your only hope of grace.

Though you must live disgraced upon the earth, cast low and trodden underfoot, while she is set on high and placed among the heavens, do not falter in your devotion. Continue to follow her whose brilliance quickens the whole world, whose very light revives all living things and calls them forth from darkness into day.

It was her own pure and burning beams that scorched you black, and by that fierce and radiant fire you were transformed. So you must remain in blackness, bound to this dark estate, until the day her kindly beams should choose to look upon you with mercy and change your darkness once again to brightness.

Yet even in your low condition, you perceive a truth she cannot escape: that an unlucky night will one day come, an inevitable hour of shadow that shall dim and darken all her present glory, however great it now appears.

For so has fate decreed, and none may overturn its law. The sun must ever have its shade attending it, and so the two of you are joined together until at last you fade as one—she to be praised forever for her shining, and you to be disdained forever for your dark.

# The Shadow's Devotion: An Analysis

This poem, structured as a series of five stanzas each beginning with the imperative "Follow," explores the theme of unrequited devotion through the extended metaphor of a shadow doomed to pursue a radiant, unattainable sun. The repetition of that single commanding word at the opening of each stanza creates a relentless, almost incantatory rhythm—a verbal echo of the shadow's ceaseless, compulsory motion. There is no escape from this imperative, no pause in which the shadow might rest or turn away. Just as a shadow cannot exist independently of the light that casts it, so too the speaker's identity has become wholly defined by, and subordinate to, the object of an impossible affection.

The central conceit is both elegant and devastating in its implications. A shadow, by its very nature, can never touch, never merge with, never truly reach the sun it trails. It exists always at a fixed remove, tethered yet forever separate. In choosing this image, the poet captures the peculiar agony of a love that is at once inseparable and unbridgeable. The beloved is figured as the sun: brilliant, life-giving, indifferent in its splendor, and utterly beyond grasp. The lover, meanwhile, is reduced to a mere consequence of that brightness—dark where the beloved is luminous, dependent where the beloved is sovereign, and always following where it can never lead.

The speaker reveals the tragic inevitability of this relationship, in which the disdained shadow must faithfully follow its beloved until both inevitably fade together, illustrating the painful yet fated nature of hopeless love. This is perhaps the poem's most poignant turn: the shadow does not follow by choice but by cosmic decree. Its devotion is not a virtue freely offered but a condition of its existence, as inescapable as the physics that binds darkness to light. The disdain the beloved shows only deepens the pathos, for the shadow persists regardless, unrewarded and unwelcomed, bound to a service that yields no return.

Yet within this bleak fatalism lies a strange and quiet consolation. If the shadow can never possess the sun, neither can it ever be wholly parted from it. Their fates are intertwined to the very end: when the sun at last sinks and its light is extinguished, the shadow too dissolves into the encompassing dark. In this final image, the poem suggests a paradoxical union achieved not in life or fulfillment but in mutual dissolution. The lovers—if they may be called such—arrive together at their vanishing, and in that shared ending the shadow attains a kind of intimacy that pursuit alone could never grant.

Ultimately, the poem offers a meditation on the powerlessness at the heart of profound love. Through its disciplined structure, its haunting refrain, and its luminous central metaphor, it transforms the experience of hopeless devotion into something both mournful and beautiful. The reader is left contemplating a love that asks for nothing because it can expect nothing, and that endures not despite its futility but as an expression of its own inescapable nature.
